newsitem.title: USA: ADT seen winner in death of Republic deal.
newsitem.headline: ADT seen winner in death of Republic deal.

text.p: ADT Ltd, the largest electronic security firm in North America, is set to capitalize on the industry's boom following the collapse of its proposed acquisition by Republic Industries Inc.
Meanwhile, the deal's termination was viewed as a major setback for Republic Industries Inc, the aggressive company founded by businessman Wayne Huizenga.
"It's apparent that Republic needed ADT a lot more than ADT needed Republic," said Andrew Jeffrey of Robertson Stephens & Co.

After nearly three months of uncertainty, Republic and ADT earlier Monday called off their $5 billion stock transaction, citing market uncertainty. The deal was troubled by Republic's volatile stock price and opposition from Western Resources Inc, which holds a 24.3 percent stake in ADT.
Just moments after the companies announced the deal was off, analysts advised investors to scoop up ADT shares.

Lehman Brothers analyst Jeffrey Kessler immediately raised his rating to a buy, citing ADT as "the single most attractive security property in an era of increasing demand by telecom/electric/cable utilities for value-added services."
Analysts appeared unswayed by the initial reaction of ADT shares, which fell 7/8 to 19. The stock was trading at about 19-1/2 before the deal was announced in July.
"Investors rarely get a second chance to buy at a discount and that's where this stock is today," Jeffrey said.
The attraction to security companies comes as other industries seek to add protection to their list of services and expand their presence in consumers' homes and businesses.
At an industry conference last week that focused on security mergers and acquisitions, ADT chief financial officer Steve Ruzika said the company was in the throes of expansion.

ADT's growth plans include this week's launch of a vehicle protection service and partnerships with Tandy Corp's Radio Shack, HFS Century 21 and other companies. Earlier this year, ADT bought Britain's Automated Security Holdings Plc.
"They've got a leading market share in a tremendous industry," Jeffrey said.

Meanwhile, the deal's collapse means that Republic will be forced to retrench as it seeks to grab market share in the security industry. Although it has bought 19 companies since it entered the market last year, all of the acquisitions have been far smaller than the proposed ADT transaction.
"Fundamentally, this deal made a lot of sense for Republic," said David Bitterman of Bear Stearns & Co.

Analysts speculated that Huizenga, a well-known dealmaker, is not prepared to give up his acquisition strategy, although the company could be hindered in the future by the same issues that dealt the fatal blow to the ADT transaction.
"There are a limited number of large players, but there are still a lot of smaller alarm players who will jump at the opportunity to take Republic stock," Jeffrey said.
Republic was not available to comment on its strategy.
In any case, analysts and investors were breathing a sigh of relief that the uncertainty in the ADT-Republic had finally been resolved.
"The good news is that we finally have an answer. It's better that they walk away now than to wait for another six months," said Randall Haase, a portfolio manager at Alliance Capital Management.

Originally valued at $5 billion, the deal's value declined sharply just weeks after the deal was struck when Republic's share price sank below $20 per share. The agreement had been based on a price of $26 for each share of ADT common stock.

The deal had been rife with uncertainty amid reports that ADT was demanding some type of price protection against volatility in Republic stock. Republic had confirmed that negotiations were ongoing, and earlier this month expressed confidence that the transaction would be completed by the end of the year.
